q: Which design task is principally under way?
o: Post-occupancy evaluation: investigating how a completed building is used.
Design development: refining and coordinating the accepted concept with physical systems.
Aesthetic styling: changing presentation appearance without physical coordination.
Initial project definition: collecting an unexplored list of owner requests.
n: The lecture distinguishes development from both initial programming and graphic polish. Actual assemblies and coordinated sections test whether the concept can coexist with structure, services and usable space. The work may refine earlier decisions, but it remains grounded in the accepted spatial intent rather than restarting with an unrelated scheme.

s: A prototype appropriate to the question
q: Which prototype best matches that purpose?
o: A complete constructed building before any feedback is collected.
An exterior image that conceals the sequence under review.
A legible plan or spatial model that lets users examine the proposed sequence.
A detailed roof-junction drawing that does not show the reception arrangement.
n: The lecture’s prototype stage develops an idea into a representation that can be evaluated. A prototype does not have to be a full-size building; it should make the relevant question understandable. Here the sequence is the test, so a representation that reveals the spatial relationships is more useful than unrelated technical detail.

q: Which response best maintains design continuity?
o: Answer only the appearance question and leave the drainage conflict unresolved.
Treat design as finished and ask the builder to select an unrecorded solution.
Approve a verbal change without reviewing its effect on adjacent work.
Clarify the intent, coordinate the technical response and communicate the resolved detail.
n: Design decisions continue during realization when actual conditions or incomplete interfaces require clarification. The lecture’s information and approval requests illustrate the need for a coordinated response. Resolve both intended appearance and technical implications, then communicate the decision clearly. This does not imply that an architect is continuously present or assumes every other discipline’s responsibility.

q: Which feature makes this a plausible parti rather than just a style label?
o: It guarantees that every alternative arrangement must be rejected.
It specifies the decorative appearance of every finished surface.
It completes all technical coordination before the first plan is studied.
It states a concise spatial idea that can guide the organization and testing of the scheme.
n: A parti is a concise organizing idea, not simply a visual theme or a completed design. The garden-and-rooms relationship can guide diagrams, massing and circulation while remaining open to testing. Its value depends on whether it helps resolve the programme, rather than whether the phrase sounds distinctive in a presentation.

q: What is missing for reliable realization of the design?
o: A general instruction asking the builder to match the rendering as closely as possible.
A material sample without information about how the components meet.
Coordinated details and specifications that explain the interface and required performance.
Another perspective showing the same junction from a more dramatic viewpoint.
n: Contract documents translate intent into instructions about components, junctions and performance. A rendering communicates appearance but may not explain assembly or water management. Coordinated details and specifications reduce guessing while retaining the desired expression. The lecture’s glass/concrete and wood/steel examples show that these interfaces are part of design quality, not merely later paperwork.

q: What is the most useful next action?
o: Review an appropriate sample or mock-up under the intended conditions before final acceptance.
Change the whole building palette without checking the specific interface.
Rely exclusively on the earlier office sample because colour never depends on context.
Accept it solely because its catalogue photograph resembles the initial rendering.
n: The lecture connects material decisions to actual conditions encountered in construction. Light, surrounding surfaces and assembly can change the result perceived from a small isolated sample. A contextual review helps determine whether the selection supports the intended character. The exercise checks the design decision rather than assuming either the catalogue image or the first impression is decisive.

q: What information best supports continuity at handover?
o: Only a list of preferred brands without plans or spatial explanations.
Only final renderings, leaving the next team to infer all priorities.
The organizing reasoning, essential relationships, agreed constraints and unresolved decisions.
A rule forbidding all development changes regardless of discovered site conditions.
n: The lecture highlights the risk of losing intent as a project passes between teams. Communicating why key relationships matter helps subsequent designers make informed adjustments when coordination or local conditions require change. Images alone may not convey those priorities. Continuity is supported by a clear record of reasoning and decisions, rather than a blanket prohibition on development.

q: How should the transition to development be handled?
o: Treat schematic acceptance as confirmation that every technical assumption is correct.
Restart all accepted decisions without identifying why they need reconsideration.
Record the accepted decisions and explicitly assign the unresolved issues for coordination.
Remove the unresolved matters from the record so the scheme appears complete.
n: Agreement helps establish a shared direction, but it does not verify unresolved technical issues. Recording open matters supports continuity into design development and prevents assumptions from becoming invisible. Some accepted decisions may later require adjustment when coordination reveals a conflict. That revision should be reasoned and communicated rather than treated as either forbidden or automatically necessary.

q: What should the team check?
o: Whether the absence of named stages means the underlying design tasks are unnecessary.
Whether every small project should copy the same layout to avoid intermediate decisions.
Whether programming, exploration, coordination and documentation tasks were actually completed despite compressed stage boundaries.
Whether producing more sheets proves that the earlier assumptions were tested.
n: The lecture notes that phase boundaries may be less visible in small projects. This does not remove the work those phases organize. A compressed workflow may be reasonable, but the team should establish whether its core decisions have been investigated and coordinated rather than mistaking a completed-looking document set for a completed design process.

q: What should happen next?
o: Assume the verbal agreement automatically updates every related drawing.
Coordinate and communicate the change across the affected information so subsequent work is consistent.
Leave the services drawing unchanged because the original conflict was architectural.
Wait for installation to reveal which version each team followed.
n: A decision can remain unresolved in practice if affected information continues to contradict it. The lecture stresses coordinated communication during realization because interfaces often cross drawings and disciplines. Updating the related information helps later work follow the agreed solution rather than reproducing a conflict that the team believed it had already solved.

s: Returning to ideation after a failed option
q: Where should the next iteration primarily focus?
o: Proceed to implementation because agreement on the brief validates the solution.
Repeat user discovery from the beginning without examining the specific layout failure.
Develop and compare alternative layouts against the confirmed requirement.
Change the requirement solely to make the existing layout count as successful.
n: Iteration should respond to the diagnosed problem. When the requirement remains sound but the chosen arrangement fails, ideating and testing another solution addresses the issue directly. This differs from a case where feedback reveals a misunderstood user need and requires redefining the problem. The loop is purposeful rather than a fixed restart procedure.

q: What should be checked before the plan is considered resolved?
o: The gross floor area, treating it as sufficient evidence that individual rooms still work.
The original single-line drawing, because it takes precedence over developed assemblies.
Net room dimensions, openings and circulation after actual assembly thicknesses are included.
Only the exterior outline, because internal wall thickness does not affect usable space.
n: Real walls occupy space. Adding structure, lining and finishes can change clear room dimensions, door positions and circulation. The lecture uses this example to distinguish development from graphic refinement. Checking usable dimensions with the actual assemblies protects the intended function and identifies conflicts before they are embedded in detailed drawings or construction.

q: Which response best follows the lecture’s empathize stage?
o: Treat the client’s permission as evidence that all user requirements are already known.
Investigate the users’ routines and needs before defining the main design problem.
Postpone user research until the construction details have been approved.
Use the architect’s own school experience as the complete user-research dataset.
n: Permission to exercise creativity does not remove the need to understand the people using a building. The empathize stage concerns investigating activities and experiences so the problem is grounded in real needs. Personal experience may suggest questions but is not a substitute for evidence about these users. That understanding informs subsequent definition and ideation.

q: Why involve the relevant consultants before the scheme becomes highly detailed?
o: Preliminary consultant advice removes the need for any later coordination.
Technical disciplines should determine the entire architectural concept independently.
Structure and services cannot influence the scheme until construction begins.
Early input can reveal constraints while the major spatial decisions are still easier to revise.
n: The lecture recommends early engagement to reduce disruptive discoveries during development. Preliminary guidance can inform available depths, member positions and service routes while alternatives are still flexible. It is not final verification: the work continues through coordinated development as assumptions are refined and actual requirements become clearer.

s: Success beyond the absence of defects
q: Which evaluation best follows the lecture’s account of design success?
o: Every usability problem must be caused by a physical construction defect.
The absence of leaks alone establishes that the architectural design is successful.
Technical defect checks and the accommodation of intended activities both matter.
User routines become irrelevant once construction quality has been checked.
n: The lecture distinguishes an absence of one type of failure from overall fitness for use. A building may perform well in one technical respect while missing the activities and relationships established in the brief. Evaluation should return to the range of objectives instead of using a single successful criterion as a complete verdict.

q: What is the strongest next design action?
o: Clarify users, activities, relationships, site constraints and resources with the client.
Issue a detailed drawing set based on a typical community centre from another site.
Fix the room layout by tracing the proportions of the preferred exterior image.
Select finishes to establish a cost baseline before identifying the required spaces.
n: Project definition translates an initial request into an architectural problem that can be addressed. User activities, space relationships, constraints and resources affect the programme. A preferred image can inform the discussion but cannot supply those missing requirements. Beginning with an untested plan risks developing a persuasive solution to the wrong problem.

q: What is the strongest recommendation at this stage?
o: Reject it solely because it differs from the original product name.
Approve it if its colour matches, leaving acoustic performance for occupancy.
Obtain performance evidence before deciding whether the alternative meets essential criteria.
Approve it immediately because its initial cost is lower.
n: Value engineering requires identifying what must be preserved and comparing alternatives against those requirements. A promising cost or maintenance advantage does not compensate for an unverified essential performance criterion. Equally, a different product is not automatically unsuitable. The decision should be based on evidence and coordinated consequences rather than price or brand alone.

q: What should the detailing response do?
o: Keep the rendered appearance but leave the physical interface unspecified.
Use the standard detail without checking what architectural intent it changes.
Resolve the technical interface while preserving or deliberately revising the important spatial relationship.
Treat the conflict as unrelated to design because it occurs in a detailed drawing.
n: Details are the technical translation of design intent. A convenient standard solution should be evaluated against the actual relationship it must realize, just as a desired image must be tested for buildability. Coordinated detailing can preserve the concept or identify a necessary revision, rather than silently replacing the intended architecture.

q: Where should the team first direct its revision?
o: Adjust the façade palette while preserving the assumed reception sequence.
Repeat the same presentation until staff become familiar with the proposal.
Move directly to implementation because the proposal has already reached testing.
Revisit understanding and definition of the workflow, then develop revised alternatives.
n: Testing can reveal a mistake in the definition of the problem, not merely in its visual expression. Here the workflow was misunderstood, so returning to user understanding and definition addresses the cause. Iteration is purposeful when the team identifies what failed. Repeating an unchanged presentation or changing finishes would leave the faulty spatial assumption intact.

q: How should they be presented for a useful decision?
o: Compare their spatial trade-offs against the agreed criteria using clear diagrams.
Choose the scheme with the more unusual outline before reviewing its circulation.
Present only the most polished perspective and omit the other scheme’s advantages.
Develop detailed finish schedules for both before discussing their basic organization.
n: Schematic design explores organizing ideas and tests how the requirements can be arranged. The lecture encourages explaining alternatives so clients understand the reasoning and trade-offs. Clear diagrams can make circulation, orientation and outdoor relationships comparable. Presentation polish should not conceal unresolved fundamentals or become the sole basis for selection.

q: What is the appropriate design response?
o: Keep the schematic column outline in the architectural drawings to preserve room area.
Reduce the column on site without obtaining a revised structural design.
Coordinate the structural requirement and revise the layout while checking usability.
Keep the original furniture layout and assume the room’s usability is unaffected.
n: Design development tests the scheme against actual physical systems. A justified structural requirement may expose an optimistic schematic assumption. The architect should coordinate the interface and reconsider room dimensions, furniture and circulation. An architectural preference does not justify silently reducing an engineered member, and leaving conflicting drawings unresolved transfers the problem to construction.

s: Early investigation proportional to the decision
q: What is the strongest response?
o: Wait because no site information can be relevant before a detailed design exists.
Assume the preferred scheme will resolve the issue without changing.
Investigate the issue early enough to support the feasibility decision it controls.
Develop final finishes first so that the investigation has a complete visual reference.
n: The lecture describes understanding becoming more detailed through design, but this should not be read as a ban on early investigation. Information must be sufficient for the decision being made. A known issue that governs viability needs attention before the team invests in a scheme founded on an untested assumption.

q: What is the architectural purpose of reviewing it?
o: Review only the drawing’s graphic neatness and ignore adjacent work.
Accept any fabrication proposal because more detailed drawings supersede the design automatically.
Treat shop drawings as unrelated to the appearance or function of the built result.
Check how the proposed fabrication and interfaces realize the coordinated design intent.
n: The lecture includes shop-drawing review among continuing design activities. The greater fabrication detail must be considered in relation to the coordinated intent and adjoining work. Review is meaningful when it identifies whether the proposed assembly preserves the required relationships, rather than treating detail level alone as evidence that a proposal is appropriate.

q: Which response should be evaluated first?
o: Lower the ceiling throughout the building without checking room requirements.
Coordinate service routes and available depth with structure and the required clear height.
Hide the duct on the architectural section because it is a consultant’s responsibility.
Retain both incompatible outlines and let the ceiling installer choose the final level.
n: The plenum example demonstrates that services occupy real space and can change the architectural result. The team should examine routing, coordination and allowable depths before selecting a response. Lowering a ceiling may be one option, but its effect on use must be evaluated. A coordinated section makes the competing physical requirements visible and supports an informed decision.

q: What should happen before the information is used for comparable pricing?
o: Ask bidders to select a system without communicating that selection to the design team.
Assume every bidder will independently choose the same interpretation.
Leave the mismatch because both systems produce a similar rendered colour.
Resolve the conflict and issue coordinated descriptions of the intended work.
n: Conflicting information can produce different pricing assumptions and different built results. Coordinating the intended system and its interfaces supports both design continuity and meaningful comparison. Similar appearance does not establish technical interchangeability. The retained lecture point is clarity of design information; no universal contractual document-precedence rule is assumed by this question.

q: Why should the cost information be revisited?
o: The evolving design should remain related to the resources available for realizing it.
Cost becomes relevant only after the design has been completely built.
An early cost statement establishes the cost of every later design change.
A change in complexity can affect appearance but cannot affect resource requirements.
n: The lecture treats probable construction cost as evolving information that helps keep design decisions connected to available resources. When scope or assemblies change, the earlier statement may no longer describe the proposal. The design lesson is ongoing comparison with constraints, without importing fee formulas or unsupported cost rates.

q: What is still needed to turn the list into a useful programme?
o: Convert each room name directly into a fixed rectangle without further discussion.
Assume rooms with familiar names have identical requirements in every project.
Interpret the rooms through activities, users, spatial relationships, constraints and available resources.
Assign a fashionable style to each room and treat the programme as complete.
n: Project definition involves interpreting requests, not merely transcribing them. A room name does not establish its activities, capacity, relationships or constraints. Clarifying those matters creates a basis for comparing schemes; otherwise the team can produce many drawings without knowing what makes one arrangement more appropriate than another.

q: Which approach best protects design value?
o: Identify the court’s essential roles and compare savings that preserve those roles.
Refuse to examine any substitution because all initial selections have equal importance.
Remove the court first because open space has no enclosed floor area.
Reduce every room and route by the same proportion without checking their functions.
n: The lecture asks designers to distinguish essential qualities from replaceable means. A court may carry several important roles that would be lost if it were treated as expendable empty space. Defining those roles allows budget alternatives to be evaluated intelligently. Preserving purpose does not require every original material or detail to remain unchanged.

q: What design lesson should be drawn from this evidence?
o: Investigate the activity and use the findings to evaluate and improve the design assumptions.
Conclude immediately that users are wrong without observing the activity.
Restore the original furniture positions before investigating why users change them.
Treat occupation as irrelevant because the construction drawings were completed.
n: The lecture presents design as continuing beyond completion and responsive to changing use. Repeated adaptation can reveal a mismatch between intended and actual activities, although its cause needs investigation. Observation and user feedback help distinguish a planning problem from other explanations. The findings can inform adjustments and future projects without pretending that a complete post-occupancy method was taught.
